[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of recent studies (2015-2025) on low-skilled immigration's wage effects on native high school graduates in local labor markets, with stratification by initial wage percentile within that group. — Evaluates whether the hypothesized polarization pattern (increased wage dispersion among less-educated natives) is consistently observed across multiple datasets and geographies, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model incorporating heterogeneous skills and endogenous task assignment within the low-skill native labor market, calibrated to match observed immigration-driven changes in wage distributions. — Provides a formal counterfactual framework to isolate the wage polarization effect from confounding factors like local demand shocks or out-migration, clarifying the causal logic.

[PATH:empirical] Card (1990) 'The Impact of the Mariel Boatlift on the Miami Labor Market' and subsequent replications — This classic natural experiment provides a direct test of wage effects of low-skilled immigration on native workers without a college degree. Recent re-analyses using updated data and methods (e.g., Peri & Yasenov, 2019) help confirm or refute the finding of null or positive wage effects in high-concentration local markets.

[PATH:empirical] Borjas (2003) 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping' and related spatial correlation studies — Borjas' work often finds negative wage effects for native high school dropouts due to immigration. Examining his methodology versus more recent instrumental variable approaches (e.g., using settlement patterns) can clarify whether the disputed positive effect holds under different identification strategies.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of U.S. low-skilled immigration wage effects (2000–2020) — A systematic review of published studies over the specified temporal and geographic scope would aggregate evidence, assess publication bias, and identify conditions (e.g., local labor market tightness, skill complementarity) under which native wages rise or fall, directly addressing the disputed hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Borjas, G. J. (2003). 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market.' Quarterly Journal of Economics. Replicate analysis specifically for high-skilled natives in non-innovation sectors. — Provides a direct empirical framework to estimate wage effects of increased labor supply from immigration, allowing decomposition by sector innovation intensity.

[PATH:empirical] Peri, G., & Sparber, C. (2009). 'Task Specialization, Immigration, and Wages.' American Economic Journal: Applied Economics. Focus on task differentiation versus wage bargaining effects. — Tests whether high-skilled immigration leads to task specialization (which could weaken wage bargaining by concentrating workers in standardized roles) versus complementarity in innovation sectors.

[PATH:literature] Dustmann, C., Frattini, T., & Preston, I. P. (2013). 'The Effect of Immigration along the Distribution of Wages.' Review of Economic Studies. Extend analysis to include union density and wage bargaining institutions as moderators. — Offers evidence on how immigration affects wages differentially across skill percentiles and institutional contexts; crucial to isolate bargaining power effects in non-innovation sectors.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic general equilibrium models of the US economy incorporating immigration, endogenous capital accumulation, and skill heterogeneity (e.g., Ben-Gad, or Storesletten) to simulate long-run wage effects — Such models test the hypothesis that dynamic adjustments (capital deepening, occupational mobility) are insufficient to offset wage depression, allowing counterfactual analysis that isolates mechanisms not observable in reduced-form empirical work.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis or systematic review of the empirical literature on long-run immigration-wage effects (e.g., Longhi, Nijkamp, & Poot) that synthesizes findings across multiple studies and contexts — A comprehensive meta-analysis can assess whether the preponderance of evidence supports wage depression across all education levels or reveals heterogeneous effects, while controlling for methodological differences.
